This bill is part of a package that would tighten rules for unions and employer groups registered under federal workplace laws.
It would create a new watchdog, the Registered Organisations Commission, with powers to investigate and enforce compliance, and impose stricter duties on officers.
The package would introduce criminal penalties for serious breaches of officer duties and increase civil fines, mirroring rules for company directors.
Establishes an independent regulator called the Registered Organisations Commission.
Strengthens financial reporting and transparency obligations for registered organisations.
Adds criminal offences and higher civil penalties for serious misconduct by officers.
Requires officers to disclose personal interests and restricts their voting and decision-making on those matters.
Broadens grounds for disqualification from holding office.
Gives the Commissioner investigation and information-gathering powers similar to those of the Australian Securities and Investments Commission.
Registered organisations, their branches, and their officers.

The government reintroduced the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill to establish a Registered Organisations Commission, strengthen financial accountability, and introduce criminal penalties for union and employer organisation officers, citing misconduct including misuse of members' funds by the Health Services Union, National Union of Workers, and Transport Workers' Union.

The speaker moved to suspend standing orders to fast-track debate on the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2014, arguing it had been thoroughly scrutinised and passed by the House of Representatives three times previously before being rejected by the Senate. The motion proposed to limit debate by allowing one opposition speaker, then the Prime Minister to conclude before immediate votes on all remaining stages.

The speaker argued that the government's motion to gag debate on the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2014 prevents new MPs from speaking on one of the double dissolution trigger bills, and moved an amendment to allow a consideration in detail stage. They criticised the government and the Leader of the House for avoiding parliamentary debate on the legislation.

The Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill was reintroduced for the fourth time, with the government arguing it has a clear mandate following the double dissolution election to improve governance and accountability of unions and employer organisations, claiming the reforms will boost the economy rather than union-bust. The bill had been repeatedly blocked by the previous Senate and was cited as one of the two reasons for the July election.

Labor argued that the Senate's amendments to the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2014 were inadequate, proposing instead that ASIC be the regulator, whistleblower protections be expanded, auditor compliance be strengthened, donation disclosure thresholds be reduced to $1,000, and volunteers be exempted—all rejected by the government, leading Labor to oppose the bill.

The Turnbull government passed the Fair Work (Registered Organisations) Amendment Bill 2014, establishing a Registered Organisations Commission with stronger enforcement powers and penalties to improve accountability and transparency for unions and employer groups. The speaker cited scandals involving Craig Thomson misusing $300,000 and Kathy Jackson fleecing over $1 million from the Health Services Union, and criticised Labor for opposing the reforms.

Christopher Pyne It is my great pleasure to sum up the debate on the Higher Education and Research Reform Bill 2014. I would like to thank all of my colleagues, particularly on this side of the House, who have given passionate and informed speeches about this reform bill over the course of the last week and a half of sittings. I thank those members of the opposition who have also participated, although I would not say their speeches were nearly as well informed as the ones from the side of the House, because they are not supporting the higher education reform bill. They are putting their head deeply in the sand and refusing to acknowledge the need for reform in higher education. It has been a very long debate. Most members of the government have participated in it. I thank my colleagues for doing this process a second time, for the second reform bill. It is because the government believes so fervently in these reforms that it has brought the bill back. The reform bill amends the Higher Education Support Act 2003 and the Australian Research Council Act 2001 to implement a fair, balanced and essential set of reforms to Australia's higher education and research system. The reform bill represents the boldest ambitions for Australian higher education in generations. It aims to make it possible for Australia to develop the best higher education system in the world. Above all, this will enable our students to get an education of the quality they need and deserve in this world of intensifying international competition. It will do so while making Australian higher education more equitable, affordable and accessible than ever before. This is the right package at the right time for Australian universities and colleges. More importantly, it is the best package for students. It has been designed thoughtfully and deliberately following careful review, consideration and consultation. All the higher education peak bodies around Australia support the core elements of these reforms.

Moved to suspend standing orders to condemn the Prime Minister over plans for $100,000 university degrees, noting the Senate had voted against the proposal the previous night, and called on the government to bring the Higher Education and Research Reform Bill on for debate so parliament could reject it again.

Introduced a revised Higher Education and Research Reform Bill after the Senate rejected the previous version, withdrawing the proposal to index HECS debts to the 10-year Treasury bond rate and adding an indexation pause for primary carers of children under five, while saying the reforms would let an extra 80,000 students a year access Commonwealth support by 2018.

Defended reintroducing the Higher Education and Research Reform Bill, arguing Labor's $6.6 billion cut to universities left them needing to replace lost revenue, and proposed students pay 50 per cent of education costs instead of the current 40 per cent, with taxpayers covering the remaining 50 rather than 60 per cent.

Opposed the higher education bill as a repeat of previously rejected policy, said the government spent $15 million advertising a package already defeated in the Senate, and cited Queensland University of Technology figures showing business students would be charged 88 per cent of their degree's cost, far above the government's claimed 50 per cent student contribution.

Backed the bill, said voting it down risked 1,700 technical and support jobs and funding for 35,000 researchers, detailed $150 million for national research infrastructure and $26 million for dementia research, and noted only three out of 20 people in her Gilmore electorate attend university against youth unemployment exceeding 50 per cent in some villages.
Voiced support for the higher education bill for the second time, accusing Labor of running a shameful scaremongering campaign to defeat overdue reform benefiting disadvantaged and regional students.

Backed the higher education bill, citing Dobell's average family income of $1,294 a week against the New South Wales average of $1,477, noted only 50 per cent of Dobell students attain a Year 12 qualification, and said the Central Coast and Hunter districts face a shortfall of 7,600 university places that a new local university precinct could address.

Opposed the bill, saying the government's total higher education cuts amount to $5 billion despite an election promise of 'no cuts to education', and cited Universities Australia modelling that course fees would need to rise 58 per cent for engineering and science and 110 per cent for environmental studies to offset the funding cuts.

Backed the bill, said HECS has applied since 1989 and Labor cut $6.6 billion from tertiary education in 2012 to 2013, and detailed new Commonwealth support for 48,000 diploma students costing $371 million and 35,000 bachelor students at non-university providers costing $449 million.

Opposed the bill's $1.9 billion in university cuts and $100,000 degrees, said the government spent more than $14 million advertising the reforms, and contrasted the University of Newcastle's 24 per cent low socioeconomic-status enrolment with 8.5 per cent at the University of New South Wales and seven per cent at the University of Sydney.

Accused Labor of hypocrisy for cutting $6.6 billion from higher education before opposing this reform, said graduates earn 75 per cent, or roughly a million dollars, more over their lifetimes than non-graduates, and noted former Labor figures John Dawkins, Gareth Evans and Maxine McKew have all backed the government's plan.

Opposed the Higher Education and Research Reform Bill, noting 39 coalition MPs voted for a blank leadership option in this week's spill, said the bill still cuts $1.9 billion from universities, and cited National Tertiary Education Union modelling showing average degrees could cost $40,000 to $65,000, with medical degrees reaching $180,000.

Supported the Higher Education and Research Reform Bill, citing University of Western Australia analysis that rural and regional students attend university at about 60 per cent of the rate of their metropolitan counterparts, and that about 50 per cent of rural students who receive offers defer them to meet financial independence requirements for Austudy.

Opposed the Higher Education and Research Reform Bill, recalling that the previous version of the bill cut $5.8 billion from higher education, criticised a $15 million government advertising campaign for the changes, and said the current bill still cuts $1.9 billion from Australian universities.

Supported the Higher Education and Research Reform Bill with amendments, said the cost of a country student living away from home can reach $20,000 a year for a family, noted La Trobe University's Mildura campus will cap fee increases at 10 per cent so a degree there will cost about $16,000, and said HECS repayments only begin once graduates earn over $50,000 a year.

Opposed the bill, criticised an $8.5 million government advertising campaign for changes that have not even passed parliament, cited Bond University's uncapped law degree costing $127,000 as evidence of what deregulation could bring, and said Universities Australia figures show an environmental science degree would need a 110 per cent fee increase to offset the funding cuts.

Supported the Higher Education and Research Reform Bill, noted the previous Labor government cut $6.6 billion from higher education while in office, said the reforms are backed by organisations including Universities Australia and the Group of Eight, and credited Senator Bridget McKenzie's Senate committee for gathering input from university vice-chancellors.

Supported the Higher Education and Research Reform Bill 2014 for its benefits to her Durack electorate, highlighting the Geraldton Universities Centre, established in 2002 and reconstituted as a cooperative model in 2010, which has graduated more than 200 students with around 200 currently enrolled, and noted providers with more than 500 Commonwealth supported places must invest 20 per cent of new revenue in scholarships for disadvantaged students.

Opposed the Higher Education and Research Reform Bill 2014, saying the government has already given up $3.5 billion of its original $3.9 billion in savings yet the bill still contains $1.9 billion in cuts to universities and $100,000 degrees, and warned the University of Newcastle alone would lose $153 million over three years.

Continued supporting the higher education reforms, noting Singapore's High Commissioner said one in 30 Singaporeans had studied in Australia, citing notable graduates including Singapore's President Dr Tony Tan Keng Yam, who completed a PhD in Mathematics at the University of Adelaide, and said Australian education exports contribute around $15 billion a year.

Opposed the Higher Education and Research Reform Bill 2014, saying it contains more than $2 billion in cuts to higher education, and cited Bond University in Western Australia as evidence that fee deregulation will push some degrees above $100,000.

Supported the higher education reforms, citing a 16 per cent decline in international education enrolments, down 130,000 since 2009 under the previous government, and pointed to published 2016 fees from the Queensland University of Technology and University of Western Australia as evidence against $100,000 degree claims.

Supported the higher education reforms, saying students will receive a 50 per cent taxpayer-funded gift toward their degree and only start repaying once earning $50,000, and cited estimates that university graduates earn 75 per cent higher incomes over their lifetime, equivalent to $1 million in additional earnings.

Opposed the Higher Education and Research Reform Bill 2014, noting the government's own claimed savings have shrunk from over $4 billion to $400 million over the forward estimates, and itemised nearly $2 billion in cuts including $171 million from equity programs and $80 million from the Australian Research Council.
The bill would force telecommunications companies to keep certain data for law enforcement and national security purposes.
It sets standard types of data to retain and a minimum retention period, and restricts which agencies can access the data.
The Commonwealth Ombudsman would oversee compliance, and the scheme must be reviewed by the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security within three years of starting.
Standardises the kinds of telecommunications data that service providers must keep.
Limits which agencies are allowed to access telecommunications data as a 'criminal law enforcement agency'.
Introduces oversight by the Commonwealth Ombudsman of enforcement agencies' access to data.
Restricts stored communications warrants to interception agencies and other law enforcement bodies with a demonstrated need.
Telecommunications service providers, law enforcement agencies, and national security agencies are affected.

This is probably the most important amendment that the Australian Greens will move during this debate. It is colloquially known as the get-a-warrant amendment. We strongly believe that in 1979 when this act was passed into law that if we had had the multitude of devices, data types and platforms that we have today, the drafters who were considering the substantial overall of telecommunications interception legislation as they were in 1979 would have looked around the field and said, 'You can tap people's phone, you can read people's email, you can track their movements around the landscape, and you can map of their social networks and find everything about their lives. These things will all be covered by a warrant and what will not be covered by a warrant is simple subscriber data so that agencies can very rapidly establish who owns the handset, who holds a particular prescription for a particular service. And so we would have ended up with the same two-tiered system that we have today, but those invasive forms of data access—whether they be tapping the phone call or reading your location as you move around the place—would have been within the warranted regime. I have no doubt about that at all. What we have seen, quite frankly, is the failure of the law to keep up with the march of technology. We still have a fairly robust warranted regime. Labor supported the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Amendment (Data Retention) Bill 2014 after securing amendments including mandatory data breach notification, encryption, a warrant regime for journalists’ data, dataset defined in legislation, and expanded oversight by the Ombudsman and Inspector-General of Intelligence and Security. The speaker argued that the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Amendment (Data Retention) Bill 2014 is vital for national security, citing that metadata is used in 100% of cybercrime investigations, 90% of counterterrorism and child protection cases, and 80% of serious organised crime investigations. Schedule 2 of the bill seeks to make significant changes to the way in which Australia will determine if it has protection obligations in relation to certain non-citizens. Specifically, the bill inserts a new section 6A that provides that a non-citizen is not entitled to complementary protection unless the person can prove that it is more likely than not that he or she will suffer significant harm if removed from Australia. Currently, the 'real chance' test means that a person must not be returned to a situation where there is a real chance that they would face significant harm.
